summary: An April 1st joke RFC. It plays with the large size of IPv6 addresses, suggesting new and "innovative" address schemes for security and cloud computing. Do not take it as a real design. It is marked experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 has so many addresses that this joke says you can do wild tricks with them, like giving every room in a huge castle a secret name.

questions: what is complex addressing in ipv6
subtitle: An April Fools' proposal to use complex mathematics for IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: Traditional IPv6 addresses are fixed-point integers, not well suited for mobile computing, cloud hosting, or solving complex addressing challenges.
tldr.mechanism: This April Fools' RFC proposes using 128-bit complex numbers (with real and imaginary parts) and floating-point mathematics to enable flexible, cloud-aware addressing schemes such as absolute, prime, geometric, and transcendental addresses.
tldr.outcome: This is a humorous April 1st document published in 2017, not a real addressing scheme.

today: RFC 8135 is an Experimental RFC published on April 1, 2017, as an April Fools' Day joke. It is not a real addressing scheme and was never intended for implementation in actual networks.

sections.title: Complex Number Addressing
sections.content:
RFC 8135 humorously proposes replacing fixed-integer IPv6 addresses with complex numbers represented as two 64-bit floating-point values (real and imaginary parts) per address. The RFC argues that the 128-bit length of IPv6 is large enough to accommodate IEEE 754 floating-point numbers, and that floating-point addressing better suits today's mobile and cloud computing environments. The real part represents the actual device location, and the imaginary part allows for cloud hosting and address flexibility.

The document plays with terminology: floating addresses for mobile devices, real addresses for fixed locations, and imaginary addresses for cloud computing where the location is not fixed. It even includes humorous advice about using duct tape to affix floating addresses to physical addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a simple number like 127.0.0.1, an address could be a fancy number with both a real and imaginary part, like mathematicians use.

sections.title: Address Types and Properties
sections.content:
The RFC describes numerous playful address categories: prime addresses (not divisible by anything except themselves) for uniqueness; composite addresses (products of primes) for shared addresses; safe addresses (with large imaginary parts) to hide real location for security; and flying addresses adapted to avian carriers using ICAO Class G airspace. It invents geometric addresses like round addresses, square addresses, and polar addresses using trigonometric transformations.

Absolute addressing solves the problem of finding the actual address by taking the absolute value (magnitude) of a complex number. Address arguments resolve disagreements by using the arctangent function on the complex address.
sections.plainLanguage: There are funny types like prime addresses (special numbers), cloud addresses (mostly imaginary), and safe house addresses that hide where they really are.

sections.title: Mathematical Tools and Implementation
sections.content:
The RFC tongue-in-cheek describes the benefits of floating-point addressing when machines are more powerful and hardware is cheaper. It notes that using complex addresses allows address arithmetic in the usual way, going beyond fixed-point limitations. The imaginary part opens up possibilities previously unavailable when floating-point hardware was expensive and limited imagination.

Implementation examples include appendices on square pi and code samples showing how to map traditional IPv6 addresses into complex addressing schemes. The RFC treats mathematical jargon (absolute, argument, magnitude, real, imaginary) as networking terminology with a straight face.
sections.plainLanguage: You can do math on addresses now: add them, multiply them, find the absolute value, or rotate them. This helps with security and cloud computing.

sections.title: Geometric and Transcendental Addressing
sections.content: The RFC proposes geometric addresses using coordinate systems and mathematical functions. A root server is described as the origin in a geometric address space. Rational addresses are fractions, irrational addresses are non-fractional, and transcendental addresses use mathematical constants like pi. The document wryly notes implementation considerations for each scheme, treating mathematical concepts as if they solve real networking problems.
sections.plainLanguage: You could use shapes (circles, squares) or math constants (like pi) as addresses.
